neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Speech fluent with normal rate and prosody. No word-finding difficulty or paraphasic errors. Naming, repetition, and comprehension intact. Recall 3/3 at registration and 3/3 at 5 minutes. Affect is flat with intermittent tearfulness when discussing symptom severity. Attention intact on serial sevens and digit span (6 forward, 4 backward).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm to 2 mm bilaterally. Visual fields full to confrontation. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact in all three divisions bilaterally. Facial symmetry at rest and with activation. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally. Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline without fasciculations.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in upper extremities bilaterally; no rigidity or spasticity. In lower extremities, the patient demonstrates give-way weakness in bilateral hip flexors and knee extensors, with strength collapsing from 4/5 to 2/5 with sustained effort. Upper extremity strength 5/5 throughout. During testing of right hip flexion, involuntary contralateral hip extension is noted (positive Hoover sign on the right). Intermittent whole-body tremor noted during examination, which is variable in amplitude and frequency, entrains to distraction testing, and diminishes when the patient is engaged in conversation.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution, with a sharp midline split at the trunk. Vibration and proprioception intact bilaterally. No extinction on double simultaneous stimulation.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. No clonus.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose intact bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing on the left is performed normally; on the right, the patient exhibits inconsistent performance with exaggerated wavering that does not follow a cerebellar pattern.
neurological_exam.gait: The patient demonstrates a markedly effortful gait with dragging of the right leg, but with inconsistent patterns — at times the leg appears to buckle yet the patient does not fall. When distracted by dual-task testing (counting backward from 100 by 7s), gait pattern transiently normalizes. Romberg testing shows dramatic swaying without falling, with improvement when patient is distracted.
neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode of bilateral upper extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds, with eyes tightly closed, side-to-side head movement, and preserved awareness (responded to name during event). The tremor increased in amplitude with attention and diminished when the examiner asked the patient to perform serial subtractions. No post-event confusion or drowsiness noted.

patient.chief_complaint: Intermittent whole-body tremor and episodes of unresponsiveness with shaking over the past 4 months, with progressive right leg weakness over the past 6 weeks
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Kowalski is a 35-year-old right-handed marketing analyst who presents to the neurology inpatient service after being transferred from an outside emergency department following two episodes of unresponsiveness with whole-body shaking in the span of 12 hours. She reports that the first episode occurred at work during a staff meeting. According to coworkers, she suddenly slumped in her chair and developed rhythmic shaking of both arms and legs lasting approximately two minutes. She was apparently responsive to her name being called during the event but seemed unable to speak. When the shaking stopped, she was tearful but alert, with no confusion or disorientation. She was taken to a local emergency department where vital signs and a basic metabolic panel were normal. She was discharged with outpatient neurology follow-up recommended.

Approximately eight hours later, at home with her partner, she experienced a second event. Her partner describes bilateral arm trembling and apparent unresponsiveness for roughly 90 seconds. Her eyes were noted to be tightly shut during the episode. She again recovered rapidly without post-event confusion, though she reported feeling emotionally overwhelmed. Her partner called emergency services and she was brought to the current hospital.

On further history, the patient describes having experienced similar episodes approximately six to eight times over the past four months. She reports that the first event occurred two weeks after learning that her position at work was being restructured, a period she characterizes as extremely stressful. The episodes vary in duration from 30 seconds to three minutes and occur without a clear consistent trigger, though she notes they seem more frequent during periods of heightened emotional distress. She denies tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or injury during these episodes. She has not been aware of any aura or warning symptom.

In addition to the episodic events, Ms. Kowalski reports progressive weakness in her right leg that began approximately six weeks ago. She first noticed difficulty climbing stairs, and the weakness has gradually worsened such that she now drags her right foot when walking. She denies any back pain, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or preceding trauma. She reports decreased sensation in the right leg but acknowledges that the numbness does not follow a consistent pattern and sometimes shifts location. She has been increasingly anxious about the possibility of a serious neurological condition such as multiple sclerosis, which her maternal aunt was diagnosed with at a similar age. She has been reading extensively about neurological diseases online, which has heightened her distress. Her sleep has been poor, with difficulty falling asleep and frequent nighttime awakenings. She denies any recent febrile illness, rash, joint symptoms, or visual changes.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive functional signs elicited and documented: Collapsing (give-way) weakness, Hoover sign, Tremor entrainment test, Non-anatomical sensory loss, Internal inconsistency on repeat testing, Dragging monoplegic gait, Improvement with attentional distraction. Functional neurological disorder is a rule-in diagnosis under DSM-5 and the criterion satisfied here is clinical incompatibility, not the absence of another disease. No further investigation is required to make the diagnosis; whatever imaging or laboratory testing is performed is for a separate, specific question.

specialized_test.impression: Cognition is within normal limits and performance validity is intact. The battery characterises the comorbidity that treatment will target — mood, anxiety, somatic symptom burden, dissociation and psychosocial context. ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) with mixed symptoms — psychogenic non-epileptic seizures and functional limb weakness

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

FND is involuntary; preserved effort on symptom-validity testing and absence of clear secondary gain argue against feigning. The rule-in signs do not distinguish FND from malingering by themselves, but the clinical context does not support a feigning explanation.

useless_tools.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

Nerve conduction studies and EMG have no role once positive functional signs are documented: the deficit is not neuromuscular, the study is uncomfortable, and a normal result reinforces the patient's search for an organic cause — the principal iatrogenic harm in this condition
Somatosensory evoked potentials answer a question about a lesion in the somatosensory pathway; a midline-splitting, non-anatomical sensory deficit is not that question

critical_actions: Do NOT make the diagnosis by exclusion: document at least one positive rule-in sign, which is the act that establishes it
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
Do not give gadolinium without a specific indication — contrast adds cost and risk and answers no question that positive functional signs have not already answered

Do not repeat the brain MRI, the laboratory panel or the lumbar puncture once a first normal study and positive rule-in signs are documented: each repetition strengthens the patient's belief that something organic has been missed
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).

Brain MRI and basic laboratory testing are OPTIONAL here, not due diligence: the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and each additional negative study is a cost and an iatrogenic harm rather than a confirmation. Where imaging is recommended in this case it is for one specific alternative question, once.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of multiple sclerosis in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-first-degree family history of MS is a weak risk factor; the patient's symptoms must be evaluated on positive findings. Normal brain MRI without demyelinating lesions effectively addresses this concern.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Reported history of psychological trauma or recent stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Use trauma history to make FND a 'foregone conclusion' without verifying positive rule-in signs
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Trauma is enriched in FND populations (Stone 2018) but is neither necessary nor sufficient for diagnosis. Positive rule-in signs remain the diagnostic anchor.

clinical_pearls: Hoover sign: involuntary hip extension on the unaffected side when testing hip flexion on the affected side — a reliable positive sign of functional weakness
Tremor entrainment: functional tremor changes frequency to match or is disrupted by voluntary rhythmic movements of another limb
Eyes tightly closed during a seizure-like event is more common in PNES than in epileptic seizures
Midline splitting of sensory loss is a positive functional sign, as true spinal or peripheral lesions do not produce exact midline split
Post-event prolactin is typically elevated 2-3x baseline after generalized tonic-clonic seizures but remains normal after PNES
